name: Wulguru
confidence_why: Wulguru ceased to be spoken before any linguist recorded it, and the only statement about its stress, in Donohue's 2007 salvage grammar assembled from 19th-century wordlists, is an explicit assumption of initial stress "on areal typological grounds" rather than an observation, while Sutton 1973 describes initial stress only for neighbouring Gugu-Badhun and says nothing about Wulguru stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is taken to fall on the first syllable of the word; this is explicitly an assumption made on areal-typological grounds (neighbouring Nyawaygi, Warrgamay, Dyirbal etc. have initial stress), not an observation, since the language is known only from 19th-century amateur written records and brief 1970s salvage notes. The assumed initial stress is used to condition high-vowel lowering.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author does note some monosyllabic words exist and that whether they were bimoraic 'cannot be determined' (sec. 1.1).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('the first syllable in a word'); no phrase-level or citation-form discussion. Evidence base is philological (Price journal, Curr 124a/b, Houze & Jacques, Gribble 1932, Tindale, Sutton 1970, Tsunoda 1972/1974), so no phonetic stress data exist in the description.
new_statements.identity_note: Donohue's sketch pools all Wulguru varieties (mainland Townsville 'Coonambella'/Nhawalgaba/Gabilgaba, Cape Cleveland = Curr 124a/b, and Palm Island Mulgu and Buluguyban), drawing mostly on Price's mainland journal; all fall under wulg1239 (no Glottolog dialect codes). The stress remark is not variety-specific and is an areal assumption, not an attested fact; a catalog entry should flag it as 'assumed by describer, language extinct c. 1900, no phonetic record'.

readall_conflicts: No source contradicts another, but no source attests Wulguru stress: Donohue 2007 (p. 6, already in the catalog) only assumes initial stress 'on areal typological grounds', and Sutton 1973 gives initial stress (with third-syllable secondary stress) for Gugu-Badhun and for the 'intact' NE Queensland type, while saying nothing about Wulguru stress. One tension is worth recording: Sutton's typology (p. 24) pairs word-initial vowels with non-initial stress in the 'aberrant' languages, and both Sutton (p. 58) and Donohue (p. 12) find genuine word-initial vowels in Cleveland Bay Wulguru from loss of initial consonants; neither author draws a stress conclusion from this, so the initial-stress reading for Wulguru rests on areal assumption, not observation, and should be marked as such.

sources.note: Only mention of stress in the whole work is inside allophonic rule 1 (vowel lowering), sec. 2.1: 'V -> [-high] / [stress] (where stress is assumed, on areal typological grounds, to apply to the first syllable in a word)'. Stress is not attested from the 19th-c. written records; initial stress is an assumption. No other occurrence of stress/accent/prosody (a full-text search for stress/accent-checked).
